extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in federalism, constitutional design, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conditions a nation should satisfy for a federal system to be practicable and durable; discusses strengths and inherent defects of federal constitutions and factors that influence their success or failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small states as cradles of political liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Small nations have therefore ever been the cradles of political liberty: and the fact that many of them have lost their immunities by extending their dominion, shows that the freedom they enjoyed was more a consequence of their inferior size than of the character of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small size makes tyranny less likely to concentrate in one individual and makes popular overthrow more feasible; evaluate whether political liberty in a polity is a function of scale and whether expansion will erode local immunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perils of great republics for republican government
rubrics_metrics.description: The history of the world affords no instance of a great nation retaining the form of a republican government for a long series of years... the existence of a great republic will always be exposed to far greater perils than that of a small one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the increased spread of destructive passions with territory (ambition, party strength) and the failure of civic virtues to scale; watch for concentration effects (capital cities, wealth inequality, lax morality, diversified interests) that threaten republican stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal system combines advantages of large and small states
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal system was created with the intention of combining the different advantages which result from the greater and the lesser extent of nations; and a single glance over the United States of America suffices to discover the advantages which they have derived from its adoption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a proposed federal arrangement genuinely splits powers so that national concerns receive centralized treatment while local, detailed administration remains provincial; look for institutional design that preserves local melioration and national strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complexity of federal systems requires informed citizenry
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal system therefore rests upon a theory which is necessarily complicated, and which demands the daily exercise of a considerable share of discretion on the part of those it governs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate population's practical knowledge of government: citizens must distinguish federal from state obligations and recognize boundaries of jurisdictions; absence of this competence undermines federal functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weakness of central (union) government inherent in federalism
rubrics_metrics.description: The most fatal... defect I have alluded to ... is the relative weakness of the government of the Union. The principle upon which all confederations rest is that of a divided sovereignty... a divided sovereignty must always be less powerful than an entire supremacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze where divided sovereignty leaves the center unable to coerce or coordinate in crises (e.g., mass state noncompliance); consider legal fictions vs. real attachments of citizens to state authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for natural causes of union beyond laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal compact cannot be lasting unless there exists in the communities which are leagued together, a certain number of inducements to union which render their common dependence agreeable, and the task of the government light ... All the people which have ever formed a confederation have been held together by a certain number of common interests, which served as the intellectual ties of association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence of common interests, economic ties, and incentives that make union attractive; law alone is insufficient—look for material and intellectual bonds sustaining the federation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of civilisation, language, and origin
rubrics_metrics.description: A certain uniformity of civilisation is not less necessary to the durability of a confederation, than a uniformity of interests in the states which compose it... One of the circumstances which most powerfully contribute to support the federal government in America, is that the states have not only similar interests, a common origin, and a common tongue, but that they are also arrived at the same stage of civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine cultural, linguistic, and civilizational homogeneity as a stabilizing factor; federations imposed on highly heterogeneous provinces are more fragile (example: Switzerland vs. US).

rubrics_metrics.name: War is the principal peril of confederations
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important occurrence which can mark the annals of a people is the breaking out of a war... War therefore renders the symptoms of the weakness of a government most palpable and most alarming; and I have shown that the inherent defect of federal governments is that of being weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate external threat environment and the center's capacity to conduct prolonged or large-scale war; if geography and neighbors make great wars probable, federal systems may fail or drift toward despotism in wartime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical position and physical strength as prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: It profits a people but little to be affluent and free, if it is perpetually exposed to be pillaged or subjugated... Physical strength is therefore one of the first conditions of the happiness and even of the existence of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the polity's geography and military/naval capabilities make it insulated from or exposed to foreign powers; favorable geography (large continent, weak neighbors) can compensate for federal weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal constitutions require citizens able to distinguish jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: I scarcely ever met with a plain American citizen who could not distinguish, with surprising facility, the obligations created by the laws of congress from those created by the laws of his own state; and who ... could point out the exact limit of the several jurisdictions of the federal courts and the tribunals of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure civic/legal literacy: everyday functioning of a federal system assumes ordinary citizens and local officials can navigate dual legal orders; lack of this ability produces administrative collisions and confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must encourage institutions promoting peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Since legislators are unable to obviate such dangerous collisions as occur between the two sovereignties ... their first object must be, not only to dissuade the confederate states from warfare, but to encourage such institutions as may promote the maintenance of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and assess institutional mechanisms (economic interdependence, arbitration, dispute-resolution bodies) that reduce incentives for interstate warfare among member states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfect central organization undermines international competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal system is not only deficient in every kind of centralized administration, but the central government itself is imperfectly organized, which is invariably an influential cause of inferiority when the nation is opposed to other countries which are themselves governed by a single authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate central administrative capacity (logistics, command, unified leadership). Weak central organization reduces ability to prosecute foreign policy and large-scale projects requiring national coordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal law may clash with state interests and provoke organized resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the federal law were to clash with the interests and prejudices of a state, it might be feared that all the citizens of that state would conceive themselves to be interested... they would instinctively unite in the common defence, and they would derive a ready-prepared organization from the share of sovereignty which the institution of their state allows them to enjoy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political dynamics when federal actions hurt concentrated state interests—risk of collective state resistance is real because states supply organization and popular loyalties that can oppose the center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal unions succeed more readily when central acts are important but rare
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union is a great republic in extent, but the paucity of objects for which its government provides assimilates it to a small state. Its acts are important, but they are rare. As the sovereignty of the Union is limited and incomplete, its exercise is not incompatible with liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design federations so central intervention is limited to truly national matters; frequent central intrusions exacerbate tensions—rarity of federal action helps preserve both liberty and cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal fictions cannot replace real attachments and affections
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of the Union depends entirely upon legal fictions; the Union is an ideal notion which only exists in the mind... the affections and the prejudices of the people are in the bosom of the states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical that constitutional language alone will secure loyalty to the center; evaluate social, emotional, and historical attachments that actually bind citizens to either state or union.
